items.note: 並 ¥600 / 大 ¥650 / 特 ¥700 / 特々 ¥750. The menu says it comes with only shredded white leek and nori, and recommends it to people who want to build their own bowl from the topping list.
並 ¥900 / 大 ¥980. The shop's note: chicken bones and chicken meat simmered a long time for a broth of pure savour — 'simple, so the ingredients show'.

items.en: Ramen in Japanese dashi rather than meat broth
items.note: 並 ¥900 / 大 ¥980. Built on several kinds of dried-fish dashi plus kombu seaweed — the menu says outright that 'the dashi is the lead role'. Lighter and more Kyoto than a typical ramen.
Lactic-fermented bamboo, seasoned — usually in soy.
The near-universal ramen upgrade: jammy yolk, white stained brown by the soy tare.
Cooked just to setting so the yolk runs — on abura-soba it works as a sauce.
'White-hair leek' — sliced into threads and soaked so it curls and stays sharp.
Plain roasted nori; dunk it and wrap noodles in it.
Belly simmered in soy and sugar until it collapses.
The small, hard-worked muscle either side of the neck — springy and unusually rich. A yakitori cut, rare as a ramen topping.
The menu describes it as 'the golden ratio of tebasaki glaze and spice' — modelled on Nagoya's famous sweet-soy peppered chicken wings.

items.en: Okayama-style fried chicken in sweet-hot glaze
items.note: The menu calls the sweet-spicy sauce クセになる — habit-forming. Okayama's regional karaage is defined by being sauced rather than dry.

items.ja: 和風ヤンニョム唐揚げ
items.note: Korean sweet-chilli yangnyeom sauce crossed with Japanese red miso — the menu's own phrase is 和韓ミックス, a Japan-Korea mix.
2 pieces ¥300 / 4 pieces ¥500 / 6 pieces ¥650, with sauces at ¥90 each — spring-onion sauce, house tartare, chilli-oil relish or kimchi. Marinated in soy, dusted in starch and fried.
One of three ¥450 mini-bowls — the others are Okayama karaage and braised pork belly — meant as a partner to the noodles.
The same soy-braised belly used as a topping, over rice.

items.ja: クリームチーズのわさび漬け
items.en: Cream cheese cured in wasabi lees
items.note: A classic Japanese drinking snack — wasabi-zuke is wasabi stems pickled in sake lees; against cold cream cheese it goes sharp, then sweet.
Skin rendered until it shatters. Confirm the seasoning — usually salt, sometimes soy.

items.ja: うずらの特製醤油漬け
items.en: Quail eggs steeped in house soy
items.note: Small marinated eggs, one bite each — the same tare that seasons the noodles.

items.ja: 水餃子（塩ダレ・ラー油）
items.en: Boiled dumplings with salt tare and chilli oil
items.note: Poached rather than fried, dressed in a salt-based sauce instead of the usual soy-vinegar.
Small ¥150 / medium ¥200 / large ¥250. Order it with abura-soba and use it to mop up the tare left in the bowl — the same idea as 追い飯 (oimeshi). Raw egg over rice (TKG) is ¥300.

tosaya_muroto.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. From the shop-managed menu page, tax included, last updated by the shop 2026-06-23.

items.note: 8 slices ¥1,800 / 4 slices ¥1,000. The reason this shop exists: a loin of skipjack scorched over blazing rice straw so the outside chars and smokes while the centre stays raw, then sliced thick. 土佐 (Tosa) is the old name for Kochi, where the dish comes from — eaten there with heaps of sliced garlic and either salt or ponzu. Ponzu contains soy sauce; ask for salt if you need to avoid wheat.

Only a few grams per bird, so it is the cut regulars order first — springy, fatty, deeply chickeny. Every yakitori here is ¥400. You will be asked 塩かタレか, salt or the sweet soy glaze; the glaze is wheat soy.
The default, forgiving cut — juicy dark meat. Often called かしわ (kashiwa) in western Japan.
Chicken minced with cartilage and aromatics for texture, packed onto the skewer. Usually bound with a little flour or breadcrumb as well as glazed in soy.
Grilled long and slow until the fat renders out and the edges go to glass. Ask for it カリカリ (karikari) — well crisped.
The grinding stomach muscle — crunchy rather than chewy, almost no fat, usually served with salt.
From the English 'hearts'. Dense, clean, slightly mineral — a good first offal skewer.
Also written レバー (rebaa). Cooked to just-pink it goes custardy; almost always finished in the sweet soy tare.
The nub of fatty meat above the tail — one per bird, and the richest thing on the grill.
Wing tip and mid-joint; eaten with fingers, worked off the two bones.
Marked おすすめ (recommended). Not chicken, but standard on any Japanese grill.

A 京野菜 — one of Kyoto's protected heirloom vegetables, bred in Maizuru around 1920. Long, thin-walled and almost entirely mild, with the very occasional hot one. Grilled whole until it blisters. Salt seasoning is fine; soy is not, so ask.
Caps grilled gill-side up so the juices pool. Ask whether it is finished with salt or soy.
Cut into blocks and charred until the middle turns to sweet slush.
Pressed tofu scored and grilled; the standard glaze is soy-based, so confirm.

items.en: Grilled broad beans in the pod
items.note: Charred whole in the pod and salted; you split them open at the table.

Egg beaten with a great deal of dashi and rolled in thin layers in a rectangular pan — the Kyoto version is savoury and wet rather than sweet. Usually seasoned with a little light soy (usukuchi), which is still wheat.
A cold block of tofu with ginger, spring onion and bonito flakes — the flakes and the poured soy are what disqualify it; ask for it plain and it is neither.
Smashed cucumber in sesame oil, garlic and chilli — the standard palate-reset between skewers.
Hirai beef is a Kochi-raised wagyu, tying the croquette to the shop's Tosa theme; the steak itself is on the menu at ¥3,850. Panko-crumbed and deep-fried — wheat throughout.
Split flat, salted and grilled — a big, oily, flaky northern fish that is a fixture of Japanese drinking menus. Salt only, no soy.

items.section: ご飯もの・麺類 / Rice & noodles
items.note: Cooked rice simmered loose in chicken broth with egg — the traditional way to finish a hotpot, and the gentlest thing on the menu.

items.section: ご飯もの・麺類 / Rice & noodles
items.note: Thick wheat noodles in the house chicken stock — the other traditional hotpot finisher.

items.section: ご飯もの・麺類 / Rice & noodles
items.note: Unseasoned steamed rice. 卵かけご飯 (raw egg over rice) is ¥660; 焼きおにぎり, a grilled rice ball brushed with soy, is ¥500.

items.en: Set course: 5 skewers plus seared bonito
items.note: The easiest way to order without Japanese. Bigger versions run ¥3,850 (8 skewers) and ¥5,500 (10 skewers plus bonito); hotpot courses go to chicken mizutaki ¥6,600, gamecock (しゃも) ¥7,700, and a winter-only kue grouper pot at ¥11,000 booked by phone.

items.section: アイスクリーム / Ice cream
items.note: Green-tea ice cream, the standard Japanese restaurant dessert. Dairy.

kyr_dashi_ryori_jifu.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. The shop's own site sells dashi kits rather than listing the dine-in menu; the dishes below were documented by visiting writers, and the day's offer is short and shifts.

items.en: Ultra-thin house noodles in clear dashi, seasoned only with salt
items.note: Also written oだしのニューめん. The whole shop in one bowl: broth from Rishiri kombu, sawara (Spanish mackerel) bushi and katsuobushi, seasoned with nothing but about one gram of rock salt from Noda in Iwate — no soy sauce at all, which is why the dashi reads so clearly. The noodles are made in-house from domestic wheat and egg only. Topped with bonito shaved to order and salt-pickled green sansho peppercorns.

items.en: Breakfast set built around dashi drawn to order
items.note: 引きたて (hikitate) means the dashi is pulled fresh in front of you. Served with tuna-bushi flakes, olive oil and salt; the second serving comes with mountain-wasabi soy sauce — that part is wheat, so decline it if you need to.

items.ja: まぐろ節のたまごかけごはん
items.en: Raw egg over rice with dried tuna flakes
items.note: TKG — the Japanese breakfast of raw egg stirred into hot rice — here made with eggs from hens fed Uji tea leaves, and dressed with salt and olive oil instead of the usual soy sauce.

items.en: Drinking dashi, served in a cup
items.note: Dashi to drink like coffee, available to take away. Kombu and dried fish with salt and nothing else. The owner opened the shop to teach people what dashi actually tastes like, partly out of alarm that Hokkaido kombu harvests have halved in fifty years.
Finished with salt rather than the usual soy, consistent with the kitchen's no-soy-sauce habit — worth confirming on the day.

items.ja: まぐろ節の和風パスタ
items.en: Japanese-style pasta with dried tuna flakes
items.note: Wheat pasta dressed in the house dashi idiom rather than a Western sauce.

Sold at the counter alongside the food — kombu and fish flakes portioned for one pot, with the owner's method: cold water with kombu and small dried fish, bring to a boil, simmer gently three minutes, then add the bonito.

kyr_chugoku_ryori_kuretake.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. The shop publishes dish names but not a full price list; the few prices below come from dated diner reports. Budget is roughly ¥1,000-2,000 a head at either meal.

items.section: 前菜・揚げ物 / Starters & fried
items.note: The plate almost every table orders. Wheat wrappers, soy-vinegar dip.

items.section: 前菜・揚げ物 / Starters & fried
items.note: Pleated cylinders of minced pork in a thin wheat wrapper, steamed rather than fried.

items.section: 前菜・揚げ物 / Starters & fried
items.note: Wheat pastry around pork and shredded vegetables, deep fried.

items.ja: 鶏の唐揚げ香味ソース
items.section: 前菜・揚げ物 / Starters & fried
items.note: 香味 (koumi) means the sauce is built on spring onion, ginger and garlic — a sharper, more Chinese treatment than plain karaage.
Tofu and minced pork in fermented broad-bean chilli paste, numbing with sansho pepper. The 四川 prefix signals they make it properly hot rather than the mild Japanese version.
Battered pork with peppers and onion in a glossy vinegar-sugar sauce. Battered and soy-seasoned — wheat twice over.

items.ja: ピーマンと豚肉の細切炒め
items.romaji: Piiman to Butaniku no Hosogiri Itame
items.en: Shredded pork and green pepper stir-fry
items.note: The Japanese-Chinese take on 青椒肉絲 (chinjao rosu) — everything cut to matchsticks so it cooks in seconds.

items.ja: キャベツと豚肉の味噌炒め
items.romaji: Kyabetsu to Butaniku no Miso Itame
items.en: Pork and cabbage stir-fried in miso
items.note: The Japanese reading of 回鍋肉 (hoikoro), twice-cooked pork. Miso here may be barley-based as well as soy.
Price seen as a 定食 set. Pork, squid, prawn, quail eggs and vegetables bound in a light starch-thickened sauce — the mildest thing on a machi-chuka menu and the standard order for children.
Served flat under a thickened sweet-sour sauce; poured over rice it becomes 天津飯.
The chilli-sauce treatment usually reserved for prawns, applied to aubergine — soft, sweet and hot. The sauce base normally contains stock and soy, so confirm before assuming it is meat-free.
Belly simmered until the fat turns translucent, in soy, sugar and spice.

items.en: Nagasaki champon — noodles in milky pork broth
items.note: A Nagasaki dish of Chinese-immigrant origin: thick noodles boiled directly in a cloudy pork-and-chicken broth loaded with cabbage, pork, squid, prawn and fish cake. Heartier and less refined than ramen, deliberately so.
Champon's dry sibling, also from Nagasaki, containing no udon at all: fine noodles fried crisp then buried under a thick seafood-and-vegetable sauce.
Sesame-and-chilli broth with minced pork. A chilled version (冷やし担々麺) appears in summer.

On from late November to early March. 酒粕 is the pressed lees left after brewing sake, and Fushimi is one of Japan's great sake districts — so this is a genuinely local bowl: thick, cloudy and faintly boozy-sweet. A 酒粕担々麺 runs alongside it.

items.ja: 五目あんかけやきそば
items.en: Fried noodles under a mixed gravy
items.note: Noodles crisped in the pan, then a starch-thickened stir-fry poured over so the top goes soft while the base stays crunchy.
The Kansai word for chahan. Egg, spring onion and pork, seasoned with soy.

One reported version: prawns and vegetables stir-fried in a light salt sauce, boiled dumplings, pickled mustard greens, egg soup, rice, jasmine tea and almond jelly. Contents rotate, and there is a 日替わりランチ (daily lunch) on weekdays.
Apricot-kernel milk jelly — the standard close to a Chinese meal in Japan. Contains dairy.

kyr_chugoku_ryori_saikaku.price_note: Prices are indicative only. The shop publishes no menu of its own; these come from diner write-ups of differing vintage (2017 onward) and have very likely risen. Treat them as a sense of scale, not a quote.

items.en: Soupless dan dan noodles — the dish people come for
items.note: A Bib Gourmand kitchen's version: sesame paste cut with Chinese black vinegar, a heap of minced pork miso and finely chopped white leek over low-hydration thin noodles that stay crumbly-firm. There is no broth — stir it thoroughly before the first bite. Diners note the black-vinegar-and-sesame pairing makes it read oddly like a spicy sauce-yakisoba.
The soup version of the same idea. Lunch runs Wednesday to Friday only and the kitchen is a one-man operation, so food and the bill can both be slow — that is the trade for the cooking.
Regulars describe the house style as 濃くない四川 — Sichuan without the heaviness: the numbing sansho aroma is all there, but the dish is not drowned in oil.

items.en: Sichuan-style simmered beef in chilli oil
items.note: Arrives still boiling. Under a drift of whole dried chillies — seasoning, not food, so do not try to eat them — sit soft starch-coated beef, mushrooms and pak choi beneath a two-centimetre float of chilli oil. The house's most aggressive dish.
Ebi-chili — a Sichuan dish rebuilt for Japanese palates in the 1950s, tomato-sweetened as much as hot.
Pork belly simmered, sliced, then returned to a hot wok with cabbage and sweet bean paste. Diners call it the strongest possible partner for plain rice.

items.en: Sweet and sour pork with black vinegar
items.note: Chinese black vinegar is aged and malty rather than sharp, so the sauce comes out dark and mellow instead of neon.

items.ja: 鶏肉の山椒唐辛子炒め
items.en: Chicken stir-fried with sansho pepper and chilli
items.note: The Sichuan 麻辣 (mala) pairing — sansho for the numbing tingle, chilli for the burn.

items.en: 'Mouth-watering chicken' — cold poached chicken in chilli oil
items.note: The name is literal: a Sichuan classic of sliced poached chicken under garlic, sansho, sesame and chilli oil, said to make you drool at the mere thought of it.
XO sauce is a Hong Kong invention of dried scallop, dried shrimp, ham and chilli — expensive, intensely savoury, and named after XO cognac purely for prestige.

items.en: Tofu simmered with leek in a mild thick sauce
items.note: The least spicy thing on the menu and, by several accounts, one of the best: a whole block of tofu with shiitake and wood-ear fungus under a gentle sweet starch-thickened sauce. Best in cold weather.

items.en: Assortment of three appetisers, chef's choice
items.note: Priced for two. One reported set: ginger-scented steamed chicken, small prawns fried and finished tsukudani-style, and edamame steeped in green-sansho soy — all built as things to drink over. The shop keeps thirty-plus bottles including baijiu, sherry and aged Shaoxing.

items.ja: きゅうりとイカの山椒オイルあえ
items.romaji: Kyuuri to Ika no Sanshou Oiru Ae
items.en: Cucumber and squid dressed in sansho oil
items.note: Named by a recent diner as the dish locals insist you order. Cold, crunchy and numbing from the pepper oil.

items.ja: まこも茸といんげん、ひき肉と芽菜の煎り炒め
items.romaji: Makomodake to Ingen, Hikiniku to Yasai no Iri-itame
items.en: Wild-rice stem and green beans stir-fried with minced pork and preserved mustard
items.note: An original the shop is known for and that diners say they have never met elsewhere. 真菰筍 (makomodake) is the swollen stem of wild rice grass, crisp like a water chestnut; dried shrimp hides in the mince.

kyr_menya_ichiki.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Read off a full-resolution photograph of the shop's own ticket machine dated 2026-04-22, the day it reopened at the new Murasakino address, so this is the newest possible card.

items.note: The house bowl and the whole reason the shop exists. Kyoto 白味噌 (shiro-miso) is pale, soft and noticeably sweet — nothing like the dark, salty red miso of Sapporo. Thick noodles, smoked chashu, a heap of green onion. Order this first if you only eat one.

items.ja: 京の白味噌 ゴマ豆乳らーめん
items.en: White-miso ramen with sesame and soy milk
items.note: Same sweet white-miso base loosened with soy milk and ground sesame — rounder and nuttier, almost like a tan-tan without the heat. Soy milk does not make it vegan; the broth is not.

items.ja: 京の白味噌 貝だしらーめん
items.note: The pricier signature: white miso cut with 貝だし, a clam/shellfish stock that adds a clean briny edge to the sweetness. The shop flags this one as its recommendation.

items.ja: 京の白味噌チャーシュー麺
items.en: White-miso ramen loaded with extra pork
items.note: チャーシュー麺 (chashu-men) anywhere in Japan means the standard bowl buried under extra slices of braised pork. Here the pork is smoked.

items.ja: 京の白味噌 ゴマ豆乳チャーシュー麺
items.en: Sesame soy-milk white-miso ramen with extra pork
items.note: The sesame–soy-milk bowl with the extra-pork treatment.

替え玉 (kaedama) is a second nest of noodles dropped into the soup you have left. Buy the ticket up front at the machine, then hand it over when your bowl is about a third full so the broth is still hot.
A whole extra nest. Same timing rule — order before the broth cools.

Also called 味玉 (ajitama). Boiled to a jammy centre then steeped in a soy-mirin marinade — the single most ordered topping in Japan. The marinade is soy-based, so it is not gluten-free unless the shop confirms otherwise.
A mound of sliced green onion. In Kyoto this is usually 九条ねぎ (Kujo negi), the local variety — thicker, sweeter and more tender than ordinary scallion, and a Kyoto vegetable in its own right.

湯葉 is the delicate skin lifted off the surface of simmering soy milk — a Kyoto temple-food speciality, and the most local thing you can add to a bowl here. It softens into the miso as you eat. Plain yuba is just soy, but ask whether it has been simmered in dashi or soy seasoning.
Genuinely plain steamed rice, unseasoned. The one safe order in a wheat-heavy shop — ask for it as-is, with no sauce and no soy poured over.

items.en: Rice bowl topped with smoked pork
items.note: Rice under slices of the same smoked chashu, with sauce. The standard ramen-shop side.
Boneless chicken marinated in soy and ginger, dusted in potato or wheat starch and deep-fried. Wheat in the marinade and a shared fryer.

items.ja: チャーシュー盛り合わせ
items.note: The chashu served on its own as a plate, to eat with a beer rather than on noodles.
The bundled add-on most people press after their ramen button — rice plus kara-age for less than buying both.

items.ja: チャーシュー丼＋唐揚げ
items.en: Pork rice bowl plus fried chicken

items.note: Beer-and-snack set, cheaper than the two apart.

items.ja: 瓶ビール＋チャーシュー盛り合わせ

items.note: 瓶 means bottle. Barley beer, so not gluten-free.
As expensive as the ramen — an unusual thing to find on a ramen ticket machine.

items.ja: ノンアルコールビール
items.note: Still brewed from barley malt despite having no alcohol.
Water is free and self-service from the counter, so you only need this if you want it.

kyr_menya_kagari_kiyamachi_t.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Taken from a photograph of the shop's current laminated tabletop MENU card dated 2026-06, the newest menu photo on its Tabelog page; the ¥950 tonkotsu price is independently confirmed by a dated June 2026 first-hand visit. An older 2018 board for this shop is still circulating online with ¥700 prices and a yuba ramen — it is obsolete, do not use it.

items.note: The card's own line: こってりなのに、くどくない — rich but not cloying. Creamy, salt-forward pork broth over thin straight noodles, heaped with Kujo green onion. The most-ordered bowl here.
鶏白湯 (tori-paitan) means chicken bones boiled hard until the broth turns opaque and thick. The card describes it as 鶏の旨味がつまったとろみスープ — a soup with body, packed with chicken savour.

items.ja: 焦がしニンニク 黒ラーメン
items.note: Black because of マー油 — garlic fried until it blackens, then blended into oil. Smoky, bitter-sweet, faintly coffee-like, and genuinely potent on the breath. The card promises you will be hooked after one bowl.

items.ja: 炙りチャーシューメン
items.note: On a separate wall sign rather than the main card, so check it is still up. 炙り means the pork slices are seared with a flame just before serving, so the fat edges caramelise.
大盛 (omori) = more noodles in the same bowl, added at the counter. The opposite, if you want less, is 少なめ (sukuname).

items.en: Upgrade any bowl to extra pork
items.note: Not a separate dish here but a surcharge on whichever ramen you chose, which buries it in extra slices. The card shows this price hand-corrected upward, so treat it as the current figure rather than a printed one.

items.en: Half a portion of extra noodles
items.note: 替玉 (kaedama) is the Kyushu-tonkotsu habit of ordering a fresh nest of noodles to finish the broth you have left. Ask while the soup is still hot.

items.en: A full portion of extra noodles

items.ja: ギョーザ 一人前6個
items.note: 一人前 means one serving; here that is six. Wheat wrappers, soy in the filling and in the dipping sauce.
Chopped chashu with Japanese mayonnaise over rice — the classic 3am order after drinking on Kiyamachi.
The chashu on its own, to go with a beer.
The jammy-yolked marinated egg — cheap here at ¥100, half what most shops charge. Soy marinade, so wheat unless confirmed.
小 = small. Unseasoned steamed rice, and the only genuinely gluten-free, vegan thing on this menu.
中 = medium. Same plain rice, larger bowl.
酎ハイ (chuhai) is shochu spirit topped with soda — here with lemon. Shochu can be distilled from barley, so ask if that matters.
Japan's default mixed drink — whisky, soda, lots of ice.
You pick the base: 麦 (mugi) is barley, 芋 (imo) is sweet potato and earthier. Say 芋 to avoid barley.
各 (kaku) on the card means 'each' — either one is ¥200.

kyr_no_ko_tonkotsu_ramen_iwa.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Read off full-resolution photographs of the shop's own ticket machine dated 2026-01, its street A-board (2026-01) and its in-store ordering card (2026-01); the ¥950 base ramen and the ¥100 spinach, ¥100 nori and ¥200 rice add-ons are re-confirmed unchanged by a dated August 2026 first-hand visit, so the card is still current.

items.note: The machine labels this ど定番!! 初めての方はまずこちら — the absolute standard, start here. 家系 (iekei) is the Yokohama style: heavy pork-bone-and-soy broth, thick chewy noodles, one slice of pork, spinach and sheets of nori. Comes with 1 chashu, 3 nori and spinach.

上 (jo) means 'upper grade'. The board itemises it: 煮豚1枚 (one braised pork slice), 燻製焼豚1枚 (one smoked pork slice), のり5枚 (5 nori), 味玉1個 (one marinated egg), spinach — ¥50 cheaper than buying those separately.
特上 = 'extra top'. Marked 店長のおすすめ (the manager's pick) and 200円お得 (¥200 of savings): 2 braised pork, 2 smoked pork, 5 nori, 1 marinated egg, double spinach.

Noodles served cold and naked with a separate bowl of concentrated broth to dunk them in, mouthful by mouthful. This one is finished with yuzu to cut the richness. The sign says 熱盛不可 — they will NOT serve the noodles warmed, so expect them chilled.

The shop's crossover: iekei broth under a Jiro-style mound of 300g of beansprouts and cabbage. 並 (nami) = regular, 180g of noodles. You get asked about garlic at the counter — see the ニンニク note below.
大 (dai) = large, 270g of noodles under the same 300g vegetable mountain. This is a lot of food; 並 defeats most people.

items.ja: ニンニク（なし／少なめ／普通／マシ／マシマシ）
items.romaji: ninniku: nashi / sukuname / futsuu / mashi / mashi-mashi
items.en: The garlic call on the Jiro bowl — free choice
items.note: On the 家二郎 only, staff ask how much raw crushed garlic you want. Answer with one word: なし (nashi, none), 少なめ (sukuname, a little), 普通 (futsuu, normal), マシ (mashi, extra), マシマシ (mashi-mashi, double extra). It is free and it is fierce — 普通 is already a heaped spoonful of raw garlic.

items.ja: 麺の硬さ・味の濃さ・脂の量
items.romaji: men no katasa / aji no kosa / abura no ryoo
items.en: The three iekei choices you are asked at ordering
items.note: The house card spells it out: when you order they ask three things, all free. 麺の硬さ (noodle firmness): 硬め katame / 普通 futsuu / 軟らかめ yawarakame. 味の濃さ (seasoning strength): 濃いめ koime / 普通 / 薄め usume. 脂の量 (fat): 多め oome / 普通 / 少なめ sukuname. If in doubt just say 普通 three times. The regulars' answer is かため、濃いめ、多め.
The standard bowl with the pork count maxed out.

items.en: Ramen with green onion and pork
items.note: ネギチャ is shop shorthand for a dressed pile of sliced green onion tossed with chopped chashu — sharp and fresh against the heavy broth.
キャベチャ = cabbage plus chashu, the same idea with shredded cabbage instead of onion.
The base bowl with 味玉 (ajitama) already in it.
大盛 (omori) = large. Bought as a separate ticket at the machine.

items.en: One slice of smoked roast pork
items.note: 枚 (mai) is the counter for flat things — one slice. The smoked version is the shop's own; it is what they lead with.
Iekei ritual: dunk a nori sheet until it goes limp, wrap a few noodles in it, eat. Plain roasted nori is gluten-free and vegan, though seasoned nori sometimes is not — these are plain.
The jammy marinated egg. Soy-based marinade means wheat by default.
背脂 (seabura) is pork back-fat, crumbled over the top so it melts into the surface of the broth. 50g is a serious amount — this is the button that makes the bowl heavy.
Blanched spinach is standard in iekei and the cheapest way to make the bowl feel less punishing. Often blanched or dressed with dashi or soy, so ask.
The onion-and-chashu mix added to any bowl.
The cheapest button on the machine. Raw white onion, diced, for a bit of bite.

items.en: Half portion of plain white rice
items.note: 半 = half. Plain unseasoned rice, and the honest gluten-free option here. Iekei tradition is to soak a nori sheet in the broth and eat it draped over the rice. Note the lunchtime sign: 11:00–15:00 rice is ¥100 off, so this drops to ¥50.

items.en: Full portion of plain white rice
items.note: The full bowl of plain rice; ¥100 between 11:00 and 15:00 under the lunchtime discount.

items.en: Green onion and pork rice bowl
items.note: 丼 (don) means a rice bowl with something on top.

items.ja: 炙りマヨキャベチャ丼
items.en: Seared mayo, cabbage and pork rice bowl
items.note: Marked NEW on the machine. Mayonnaise blowtorched until it browns, over cabbage and chashu on rice.
The shop's smoked chashu over rice, sold as its own dish.

items.ja: 瓶ビール（プレモル小瓶）
items.en: Small bottle of Premium Malt's beer
items.note: 小瓶 = small bottle. Barley beer.

kyr_aburasoba_daikakumei_kin.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. This shop runs TWO ticket-machine panels and swaps between them, so treat the lineup as unstable. The 油そば panel below is read off photographs from roughly 2025-09, corroborated by a dated August 2025 visit and by a May 2026 diner who ordered 「普通の油そば」, so it is still live. The あえ麺 panel (釜玉 / 肉みそ / 肉玉) is read off a separate photograph from roughly late 2025, and a 2026-04 reviewer describes the shop as having had a リニューアルオープン. Expect one of the two panels on any given visit; check before queueing.

items.en: Brothless noodles in tare and oil
items.note: There is no soup. A pool of soy tare and chilli-scented oil sits hidden in the bottom of the bowl under the noodles, with chashu, shredded nori, menma and sesame on top. The shop's own instructions: first splash 酢 (su, vinegar) and ラー油 (rayu, chilli oil) once or twice around the rim from the table bottles, then mix hard — flipping the noodles over — until the tare is evenly through and no dry patches remain. Only then start eating. They also suggest 黒酢 (black vinegar) as it pairs with the garlic.
半熟 (hanjuku) means half-cooked — a soft-boiled egg with a runny centre. Break it into the mix and the yolk turns the tare creamy.
肉盛り = a mound of meat. Four chashu slices instead of the standard two, fanned right across the bowl.

全部のせ (zenbu-nose) literally 'everything placed on' — the shop's own poster explains this one is the standard bowl plus a soft-boiled egg AND four chashu slices. If you can't read the machine and want the full experience, this is the button.

学生 (gakusei) = student. An orange band across the machine marks the 学割料金 (student rate) row — Ritsumeikan University is a few minutes away. The whole row is ¥100 off: 半熟玉子 ¥800, 肉盛り ¥900, 全部のせ ¥1,000. You need to be a student; expect to be asked.

From the second, あえ麺 (aemen, sauce-tossed noodle) panel. 釜玉 borrows the udon idea: hot noodles tossed straight with raw egg so it thickens into a carbonara-like coating, here with pork and sesame. The button notes you can swap 味ネギ for 花かつお (bonito flakes).

Minced pork cooked down with miso and chilli over the noodles with an egg yolk and chives. The button says the 肉みそ（辛） can be served 別皿 — on a separate plate — if you want to control the heat, and that a 釜玉 topping also suits it.
The top of the aemen panel — sliced pork blanketing the noodles with a yolk in the middle.

items.ja: 全あえ麺に玉子が入っております
items.romaji: zen aemen ni tamago ga haitte orimasu
items.en: Every aemen contains egg — tell staff if you can't have it
items.note: A printed strip runs the width of the aemen panel: 全あえ麺に玉子が入っておりますので苦手な方はスタッフにお申し出ください — every aemen has egg in it, so tell staff if that is a problem. Worth knowing before you press a button if you avoid egg.
The aemen panel has its own student row: 釜玉 ¥700, 肉みそ ¥850, 肉玉 ¥900.

The portion buttons sit at the very top of the machine, so press your bowl first and then one of these. 大盛 is the ordinary 'large'. On the aemen panel this is handled differently — a sign says ordering 並 (regular) lets you change up to 大盛 or W盛 free by asking staff.
Twice the noodles. Since there is no broth to fill you up, regulars say the standard size runs small and double is very manageable.
Three times the noodles, same price per step. Genuinely large. Present on both panels.

items.en: Lunch set — fried chicken plus rice
items.note: The small label under the button reads からあげ3つ・TKGか白ごはん: three pieces of fried chicken plus either the raw-egg rice or plain rice.

items.en: Value set — rice plus fried chicken
items.note: The aemen panel's equivalent: a bowl of rice and a portion of kara-age.
Plain unseasoned steamed rice — the one genuinely gluten-free and vegan item here, and priced the same on both panels. Keep it separate from the noodle bowl if that matters to you.

items.en: A 50g scoop of rice for the leftover sauce
items.note: The machine explains it: チョイ飯（50g）とは？食べ終わった油そばのタレにご飯を入れて食べるタレご飯 — a small scoop of rice you tip into the tare left in the bottom of the bowl once the noodles are gone, then stir and eat. This is the ending the shop wants you to have, and it costs ¥50. The rice itself is plain, but the sauce it soaks up is wheat soy.
Soy-and-ginger marinated chicken, starch-coated and deep-fried. Priced ¥250 on the aemen panel and ¥300 on the abura-soba panel, so expect either.

items.ja: ヤンニョム風 唐揚げ
items.note: On the aemen panel only. The same kara-age tossed in a 양념 (yangnyeom) sweet-garlic-chilli glaze. Gochujang normally contains wheat.

items.en: Fries plus two pieces of fried chicken
items.note: On the abura-soba panel. The machine spells it out: ポテト＆唐揚げ2ヶ — potato fries and two kara-age, sharing the fryer.
炙り = flame-seared. Chashu blowtorched over rice.
On the aemen panel. Chopped chashu with Japanese mayonnaise over rice.

TKG is the standard abbreviation for 卵かけご飯 — a raw egg cracked over hot rice and stirred, usually with a splash of soy. A completely ordinary Japanese breakfast, and here the recommended finish: the shop's poster says pour the leftover tare in too and add the raw egg for the perfect ending. On both panels at ¥200.

items.ja: トッピング 半熟玉子／生卵
items.en: Add a soft-boiled egg, or a raw one
items.note: The pink-labelled row along the bottom of the machine is all toppings. 半熟玉子 (soft-boiled) is ¥100; 生卵 (nama-tamago, raw) is ¥50. Japanese eggs are produced to be eaten raw — crack it straight into the mixed noodles and it coats everything. The soft-boiled one is usually soy-marinated, so ask if gluten matters.

items.ja: トッピング メンマ／キムチ
items.note: メンマ (menma) is bamboo shoot fermented then simmered in seasoning — the crunchy pale sticks in almost every ramen bowl, usually simmered in soy and often dashi. キムチ is Korean fermented cabbage, commonly containing fish sauce or salted shrimp. Both ¥100.

items.ja: トッピング チャーシュー
コーラ or オレンジ
items.note: One button, your pick of the two.
Barley beer. The aemen panel also carries チューハイ ¥400 and ハイボール ¥450, though both were showing sold-out lamps when photographed.

kyr_yume_wa_chikara_nari.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Read off a photograph of the shop's ticket machine dated 2026-06, plus its counter cards dated 2026-05 and 2026-07. The shop rebuilt the machine some time after October 2025: it used to be organised by noodle weight and pork-slice count (200g/300g × 豚1枚/豚2枚) and is now organised by FLAVOUR at a flat 200g. Older listings showing the 豚1枚/豚2枚 grid are obsolete. ¥1,000 for a 200g bowl is confirmed by a dated June 2026 first-hand visit.

items.note: The default bowl and the one most people order. 二郎系 (Jiro-style) means a soy-and-pork-fat broth under a mountain of boiled beansprouts and cabbage, with 豚 (buta) — not delicate chashu but thick fatty slabs of braised pork. Every bowl is 200g of 全粒粉超極太麺, wholemeal ultra-thick noodles, which the shop makes itself. Their own chart: a standard ramen is about 150g, so 200g is roughly 1.5 servings.

汁なし (shirunashi) = 'no soup'. Same mountain of vegetables and pork, but the tare and fat sit at the bottom of the bowl instead of a broth — mix hard from underneath before the first bite. Regulars add a raw egg to dip into.

塩 (shio) = salt rather than soy as the seasoning base. Cleaner and lighter-tasting than the shoyu, though still a heavy pork bowl. Shio tare often still contains some soy or wheat-derived seasoning, so it is not a gluten-free route without asking.
担担 (tantan) is the Sichuan-derived sesame-paste and chilli style, here built on the Jiro frame. Nutty, numbing and rich.
汁なし担担麺 is a dish in its own right across Japan — thick sesame-chilli paste at the bottom, mixed up through the noodles.
辛味噌 = spicy miso. Miso can be barley-based (麦味噌), a second wheat-family risk on top of the soy.
梅 (ume) is the salted, intensely sour Japanese pickled plum. An unusual thing to meet in a Jiro bowl — the sharp acidity cuts straight through the fat, which is exactly the point.

items.ja: やさい・あぶら・にんにく（コール）
items.en: The counter call — the three free choices
items.note: This is the moment travellers panic. As your bowl is handed over, staff ask three things IN THIS ORDER: ① やさい (yasai, the beansprout-and-cabbage mountain) ② あぶら (abura, melted pork back-fat spooned on top) ③ にんにく (ninniku, raw crushed garlic). For each, answer with one word — なし (nashi, none) / 少なめ (sukuname, less) / 普通 (futsuu, normal). All three of those are FREE. If you want more than normal, マシ (mashi) and マシマシ (mashi-mashi) must be bought as tickets at the machine first — you cannot call for them at the counter.

items.ja: 野菜マシマシのルール
items.en: House rules on ordering the biggest vegetable pile
items.note: A hand-written board next to the machine sets three conditions: 初来店の方はひかえて下さい — first-time visitors should NOT order マシマシ; 購入後の返金はしません — no refunds once bought; 食べ残しは追加料金いただきます — leaving food unfinished incurs an extra charge. Read as friendly but meant seriously. On a first visit, answer 普通.
豚 (buta) here means the thick fatty braised pork block, not thin chashu. This button upgrades you to a bigger piece.

Takes the bowl from 200g to 300g. Going the other way is free but must be done in person: the machine's sign says 麺の量を減らされるお客様は食券を買わないでお席で直接ご注文ください — if you want LESS noodle, do not buy a ticket, order at your seat.

items.en: Extra vegetables — one step or two
items.note: The button carries two levels: 1枚マシ (one step up) and 2枚マシマシ (two steps). Boiled beansprouts and cabbage, piled well above the rim at the top level.

items.en: Extra pork back-fat — one step or two
items.note: Same two levels, 1枚マシ and 2枚マシマシ. Melted back-fat spooned over the top, which is what makes a Jiro bowl heavy.
A Jiro-style habit that sounds wrong and works — it melts into the fat and tare.
Served in a small dish. On the brothless bowls, dip the noodles into it sukiyaki-style; on the soup bowls, crack it in.

Bottom-right button on the machine. The label says 内容、金額はSNSで告知 — what it is and what it costs are announced only on the shop's social media, so check that before you go. The shop also runs frequent handwritten 限定 (gentei, limited) boards by the door: recent ones have included a summer ユメメカ風ピビン麺, a cold lemon-and-corn tantan, and a 500g noodle challenge.

items.ja: 豚なし ご希望のお客様
items.en: Skip the pork, take ¥200 of toppings instead
items.note: A yellow counter card: if you do not want the pork slab, you may pick ¥200 worth from the list below free — just say so when you put your ticket down (食券を置かれた際にお声かけ下さい). Note this does NOT make the bowl vegetarian; the broth and tare are still pork-based.

items.ja: 味変しょうが／カレー／マヨネーズ／ゆずこしょう
items.note: 味変 (aji-hen) means 'flavour change' — something stirred in halfway through so the second half tastes different. Ginger cuts the fat; curry and mayonnaise enrich it; 柚子胡椒 is fermented green chilli with yuzu peel and salt, and despite the name contains no black pepper. Japanese curry roux contains wheat flour; mayonnaise is egg-based.
Sliced green onion, fresh against all that fat.
ちょい (choi) means 'just a bit'. Fried rice is wok-fried with soy sauce, so unlike plain rice it is not gluten-free.
黒ウーロン茶 is a more heavily oxidised oolong sold in Japan as a cut-through-grease drink, which is why a Jiro shop stocks it.

items.ja: 卓上調味料（カエシ・酢・一味・ブラックペッパー）
items.note: Four bottles, all free. カエシ (kaeshi) is the concentrated soy tare — the card says use it 味が薄い時に, when the bowl tastes flat; it is wheat soy. 酢 (su) vinegar cuts the fat. 一味 (ichimi) is pure ground red chilli. Plus black pepper. When you finish, put the bowl, cup and chopsticks up on the counter and bin your tissues in the black bin behind you.

kyr_menya_roman.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Taken from the shop's own official site and the shop-managed menu page it links to, cross-checked against photographs of the shop's own bilingual street A-boards dated 2026-01, the month it opened.

items.note: The house bowl. 鶏白湯 (tori-paitan) is chicken bones boiled hard for hours until the broth emulsifies into something opaque and almost soupy-thick. The shop uses さつま知覧どり, Kagoshima hens raised 450 days — older birds, deeper flavour — simmered with vegetables into what they call their 黄金スープ, golden soup. Give it a stir before the first spoonful; it separates.

items.ja: 極上 鶏チャーシュー麺
items.en: Deluxe ramen loaded with chicken chashu
items.note: 極上 (gokujo) = 'finest'. Flagged by the shop as 人気NO.1, their best seller: the paitan bowl covered in slices of low-cooked chicken chashu rather than pork.

items.ja: 京都九条ネギラーメン
items.en: Ramen heaped with Kyoto Kujo green onion
items.note: 九条ねぎ (Kujo negi) is Kyoto's own green onion, named for the Kujo district and grown here for over a thousand years — thicker, sweeter and softer than ordinary scallion, with a slippery gel inside the leaf. Piled on in a green mound over the chicken broth. The most local order on this menu.

items.ja: 和牛ラーメン【黒毛和牛 A5ランク】
items.en: Ramen topped with A5 wagyu beef
items.note: 黒毛和牛 is Japanese Black, the main wagyu breed; A5 is the top grade for marbling. Slices are laid over the hot broth so they cook only just through. Nearly three times the price of the standard bowl — an occasion dish, not a normal ramen order.

items.ja: 鶏チャーシューもやし
items.note: 逸品 (ippin) heads this section — 'choice items', the small plates. Sliced chicken chashu over dressed beansprouts.
Fried chicken tossed in 양념 (yangnyeom) sauce — sweet, garlicky, moderately spicy, sticky. Gochujang chilli paste normally contains wheat, and the chicken is battered.

items.ja: とり南蛮 しば漬けタルタル
items.en: Sweet-vinegar fried chicken with Kyoto-pickle tartare
items.note: チキン南蛮 is fried chicken dipped in sweet vinegar sauce and topped with tartare — a Miyazaki dish. The Kyoto twist here is しば漬け (shibazuke), the purple-red pickle of eggplant and cucumber cured with red shiso, chopped into the tartare. Battered and soy-seasoned.
とろとろ means so soft it collapses. 豚足 (tonsoku) is pig's foot, slow-braised until the collagen goes to jelly — an izakaya classic, mostly skin and gelatin rather than meat.
The cheapest thing on the menu, and a good palate-cutter against the thick broth. Kimchi seasoning commonly contains fish sauce or salted shrimp.
Marinated in soy and ginger, starch-coated, deep-fried. The default beer companion in Japan.
せんべい normally means a rice cracker; here it describes the texture — chicken skin pressed and fried until it shatters like one. Salty, very crisp.

items.ja: 和牛ユッケ重【A5黒毛和牛】
items.note: ユッケ (yukke) is the Korean-Japanese raw seasoned beef, usually with a raw egg yolk on top; 重 (ju) means it is served in a lacquered box over rice. Raw beef — worth knowing before you order. Seasoned with soy.
The shop's chicken chashu over rice with an egg yolk — the standard side to a ramen here.

items.en: How to order — by QR code on your phone
items.note: There is no ticket machine to puzzle over and no Japanese-only menu to read: the shop posts bilingual instructions. ① Scan the QR code at the counter and pick your items and toppings from the phone menu. ② Sign in to confirm the order — Apple ID, Google account and LINE all work. ③ Pay on the phone. ④ Hold the resulting QR code up to the ticket printer, take the printed 食券 (meal ticket) and hand it to staff. Only 8 seats, so expect to wait at busy times.

ChIJxaEJ-r0HAWARd97A1vZKx5A.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Read from a photograph of the shop's own laminated table menu card, May 2026.

items.section: 造り・冷菜 / Sashimi & cold dishes
items.note: Raw salmon, sliced. Comes with soy sauce on the side — Japanese soy sauce is wheat-based, so ask for it left off if that matters.

items.en: Chopped raw tuna 'yukhoe' with a raw egg yolk
items.section: 造り・冷菜 / Sashimi & cold dishes
items.note: Korean-style: diced raw tuna in a sesame-soy dressing with a yolk on top and shredded nori. Stir it together before eating.
The shop's headline fried dish — a local YouTube review is literally titled after it. Wheat-flour dredge.
The default izakaya order. Marinated in soy and ginger, dredged in wheat flour or potato starch, fried to order.
Tiny whole squid, eaten head and all — briny and slightly bitter inside. A spring speciality that this shop keeps on.
本 (hon) is the counter for long thin things — here it means 2 wings.
Finger-length whole fish, eaten bones and all with a squeeze of lemon.
Cheap Showa-era pub food: a thick slice of ham in panko. コ/個 (ko) is the counter for pieces.
Panko crumb plus a wheat-and-fruit brown sauce — doubly not gluten-free.

1 skewer ¥200, 2 skewers ¥350. ぼんじり is the small fatty nub above the tail — rich and juicy, a connoisseur's cut. 串 (kushi) = skewer, so 1串/2串 is how many. Ask for 塩 (shio, salt) rather than タレ (tare) — tare is a wheat-soy glaze.

items.en: Chicken tenderloin wrapped with shiso leaf
items.note: 1 skewer ¥180, 2 skewers ¥300. ささみ is the lean breast fillet; shiso (perilla) gives it a minty-basil lift. Usually salt-grilled, but confirm no soy glaze.
Charcoal-grilled frankfurter. Sausage casings and fillers routinely contain wheat.

A Kyoto speciality — the silky film lifted off simmering soy milk, eaten cold with a dab of soy and wasabi. The soy skin itself is fine; the dipping sauce is the wheat risk, and it may be dashi-based rather than plain soy.
Whole garlic cloves cured in a red-shiso pickle — sharp, sweet-sour, a drinking snack. Pickling liquid often contains soy sauce or bonito extract.
Yes, whale — still an old-school izakaya staple in Japan. Dark, dense, beef-like meat simmered in soy and ginger. Worth knowing what you are ordering.

items.en: Pacific saury simmered with sansho pepper
items.note: Oily autumn fish cooked down in soy until the bones are soft; sansho gives a citrusy, tongue-tingling numbness.

items.en: Fermented soybeans with grated mountain yam
items.note: Two famously slimy things at once. Natto is pungent and stringy, tororo is a slippery grated yam. The sachet dressing usually contains both wheat soy sauce and bonito dashi.
Cold pink duck breast fanned over leaves. The dressing is the gluten question.

items.ja: 釜あげしらすとキューリの酢のもの
items.romaji: kamaage shirasu to kyuuri no sunomono
items.en: Boiled baby whitebait and cucumber in sweet vinegar
items.note: 酢の物 (sunomono) is the palate-cleanser course — cold, sharp, refreshing. しらす are tiny translucent whole fish.

items.ja: みつ葉ともやしのおひたし
items.en: Blanched mitsuba herb and bean sprouts in dashi
items.note: おひたし = greens briefly blanched then steeped in seasoned stock. Mitsuba tastes like a cross between parsley and celery. The steeping liquid is bonito dashi plus soy — so not vegan and not gluten-free by default.
Charred whole until collapsing, skin slipped off, served with ginger and soy. Almost always finished with bonito flakes.
A sac of tiny salted roe, spicy and intensely savoury — eaten in small bites with rice or drink. The curing liquid usually contains soy and sometimes wheat.
A Kansai variety so tender and juicy it is eaten raw, torn by hand. Usually served with a soy or dashi dip.
A block of firm tofu fried so the outside is golden and chewy, then grilled and topped with ginger and spring onion. Plant-based in itself — the poured-over sauce and bonito flakes are what break it.

kyr_nibodamashii_ramen_gion_.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Read from a full-resolution photograph of the in-store menu sheet.

items.note: The whole shop is this bowl. Broth built on dried baby sardines with heads and guts left in, so it keeps a real bitter edge — oceanic and savoury, the taste niboshi fans chase and everyone else finds strange. A whole dried sardine sits on top as a garnish. The shop romanises its name NIBO-TAMA on the menu.

items.en: Deluxe niboshi ramen — same bowl plus 3 sheets of nori and a marinated egg
items.note: 特製 (tokusei, 'special') on almost any Japanese ramen menu means the loaded version. Here the extra ¥300 buys exactly 3 sheets of nori and one ajitama.

items.en: Brothless niboshi noodles — noodles tossed in seasoned oil and tare
items.note: 油そば (abura-soba) arrives with no soup: a pool of flavoured oil and tare at the bottom of the bowl. Mix hard from the bottom before the first bite. The table vinegar and chilli are meant for it.
大盛り (oomori) = extra noodles. Here it costs nothing, so say 大盛りで (oomori de) when you order if you are hungry. 並 (nami) would be the regular size.
Also written 味玉 (ajitama) at most shops — a jammy-yolked egg steeped in soy tare. The single most-ordered ramen topping in Japan.
Dip a sheet into the broth to soften, then wrap a mouthful of noodles in it.
A heap of raw sliced green onion — cuts through the oil of a niboshi bowl.
Ferociously sour and salty. Unusual on ramen — it works with the sardine broth. Some are cured with bonito or soy.
Japanese-market kimchi commonly contains fish sauce or salted shrimp, and the seasoning can carry wheat.
The braised pork belly or loin slices. On most menus the pre-loaded version is called チャーシュー麺.
Melts into the oil of the abura-soba rather than the ramen — that is how regulars use it.

items.en: Rare-cooked pork over rice, small bowl
items.note: 生 here means the pork is cooked low and slow so it stays pink and soft, laid over rice with a yolk. A ¥500 mini bowl, not a full meal.

items.en: Rice topped with dried sardine, nori and chilli
items.note: いりこ is the western-Japan word for the same dried sardines the broth is made from. The house move: eat half, then tip the rest into the leftover ramen broth.
卵かけご飯 abbreviated. Crack the raw egg on hot rice, add the soy tare, stir until glossy. A national comfort food — eggs are safe to eat raw in Japan. The tare is wheat soy.
中瓶 is the standard 500ml izakaya bottle. Price not legible on the menu photo.

items.ja: ソフトドリンク（ウーロン茶・緑茶・ジャスミン茶・紅茶）
items.en: Soft drinks — oolong tea, green tea, jasmine tea, black tea
items.note: Price not legible on the menu photo.

items.ja: 卓上調味料（一味タレ・黒胡椒・ホワイトペッパー・煮干し酢）
items.en: On-table seasonings: chilli tare, black pepper, white pepper, niboshi vinegar
items.note: The 煮干し酢 (sardine vinegar) is the unusual one — a splash sharpens the bitterness partway through. The chilli tare is soy-based.

kyr_chuka_rokuroku.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. From the shop's printed menu book and its current handwritten lunch board, photographed August 2026. A 2023 board circulating online is ¥140 lower on the tantanmen — do not use it.

items.section: お昼のお品書き / Lunch board
items.note: 定食 = a main plus rice, soup and a side, priced as one. Changes weekly (a recent one was pork and wood-ear with egg). ¥1,300 with the almond jelly dessert added.

items.en: Dan dan noodles set, with rice or almond jelly
items.section: お昼のお品書き / Lunch board
items.note: ¥1,000 for the bowl alone. This shop's version is famously sour as well as numbing-hot — heavy on minced pork, pak choi and Sichuan pepper. Ask for it 汁なし (shirunashi, brothless) if you prefer.

items.ja: チャーシューと葱の広東風あえ麺Set
items.romaji: chaashuu to negi no kanton-fuu aemen setto
items.en: Cantonese-style tossed noodles with roast pork and spring onion, set
items.section: お昼のお品書き / Lunch board
items.note: あえ麺 (aemen) = no soup, noodles tossed in sauce and oil. ¥1,100 as a single dish.

items.ja: チャーハン（スープ・杏仁豆腐付）
items.en: Fried rice, with soup and almond jelly
items.section: お昼のお品書き / Lunch board
items.note: チャーハン and 焼めし mean the same thing — wok-fried rice with egg and pork. Seasoned with soy, so wheat.

items.ja: 魯肉飯（スープ・杏仁豆腐付）
items.en: Taiwanese braised pork over rice, with soup and almond jelly
items.section: お昼のお品書き / Lunch board
items.note: Lu rou fan — finely chopped fatty pork slow-braised in soy, five-spice and rice wine, ladled over rice. Sweet, sticky, deeply savoury.

items.en: Crisp-fried noodles under a thick five-ingredient gravy, set
items.section: お昼のお品書き / Lunch board
items.note: 五目 (gomoku) = 'five things', i.e. mixed. あんかけ = a starch-thickened glossy sauce poured over. ¥1,400 as a single dish. The noodles go from crunchy to soft as you eat.

items.ja: 細切り豚肉とザーサイのあんかけ汁そば
items.romaji: hosogiri butaniku to zaasai no ankake shiru-soba
items.en: Noodle soup with shredded pork and pickled mustard stem in thick gravy
items.section: お昼のお品書き / Lunch board
items.note: ザーサイ (zha cai) is a crunchy salty Sichuan pickle. ¥1,200 without the rice or dessert.

items.section: お昼のお品書き / Lunch board
items.note: 冷やし = served cold, a summer-only listing. ¥1,200 alone.

items.en: Cold Chinese-style noodle salad with mixed toppings, set
items.section: お昼のお品書き / Lunch board
items.note: 冷やし中華 is the Japanese summer classic: chilled noodles fanned with ham, egg strips, cucumber and a tart soy-vinegar dressing. ¥1,400 alone.
Silky-skinned wontons floating alongside the noodles.

items.en: Noodle soup buried under shredded spring onion
items.note: そば on a Chinese menu means wheat ramen noodles, not buckwheat. A mound of raw shredded negi on top.
からし is hot Japanese mustard — sinus-clearing rather than chilli-hot. A Kyoto-specific noodle genre.
The Kansai word for chahan. Same dish.
Genuinely gluten-free and vegan as long as it is plain — not fried, not seasoned. The safest thing on the menu.

items.en: Pan-fried pork dumplings with a lacy crisp 'wing', 5 pieces
items.note: 羽根 = the wing: a starch slurry poured into the pan sets into a crisp golden web joining the dumplings. Snap it apart at the table.
水 = water, i.e. boiled rather than fried. Thicker, chewier skins than the pan-fried version.
Open-topped steamed dumplings with a chilli-oil kick. A shop signature.

Lo bak go — grated daikon set with rice flour and dried shrimp or sausage, then sliced and fried until the outside crusts. Rice-flour based but usually contains wheat starch and is fried on a shared surface.
パリパリ is the onomatopoeia for a thin, brittle crunch.

items.en: Fried chicken under a sweet-sour spring-onion soy dressing
items.note: You lin ji — crisp chicken doused at the last second in a vinegared soy-and-negi sauce, so the skin is half crisp, half soaked.

items.en: Mapo tofu — soft tofu and minced pork in a numbing chilli bean sauce
items.note: The numbness is Sichuan pepper (花椒), separate from the chilli heat. Fermented broad-bean paste and soy both carry wheat, and there is pork mince in it.

items.ja: 大徳寺 小川豆腐さんのプレミアム麻婆
items.en: Premium mapo tofu made with tofu from Ogawa Tofu of Daitoku-ji
items.note: The upgrade uses tofu from a named local maker beside Daitoku-ji temple, a few minutes from the shop. Worth the ¥100 if you like tofu.
Crunchy, salty, chilli-flecked pickle — the cheapest thing to put on the table with a beer. Usually dressed with sesame oil, sometimes soy.
Not tofu despite the name — a soft milk-and-apricot-kernel jelly, the standard Chinese-restaurant dessert. Contains dairy and usually gelatin.

kyr_otabi_hanten.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Read from both sides of the shop's printed お献立表, photographed at full resolution, March 2025.

items.note: The plainest bowl in the house and the cheapest way in. Adding butter to any ramen here is +¥50.
Clearer and lighter than the soy version — same noodles and stock, different tare.
Thicker and sweeter. Note that miso itself is sometimes barley-based (麦味噌) on top of the wheat noodles.

items.en: Ramen loaded with extra roast pork slices
items.note: The standard upgrade at any Japanese ramen shop: same bowl, the surface covered in pork.

items.ja: 御旅ラーメン（ピリ辛あんかけ麺）
items.en: House ramen — noodles under a mildly spicy thickened gravy
items.note: ピリ辛 = gently spicy, not punishing. あんかけ = the glossy starch-thickened sauce, which keeps the bowl scalding hot far longer than it looks.

items.en: Ramen topped with a crab omelette in sweet-sour gravy
items.note: 天津 (Tenshin/Tianjin) on a Japanese Chinese menu always means a fluffy egg omelette with crab stick under a thick sweet-vinegary sauce.

items.en: Nagasaki-style noodles with pork, seafood and cabbage, soy version
items.note: Everything stir-fried then simmered together with the noodles in one bowl — vegetables, squid, pork, fish cake. A meal in itself.

items.ja: 皿うどん（揚げ麺五目あんかけ）
items.en: Crisp fried noodles under mixed seafood-and-vegetable gravy
items.note: Despite the name it is not udon — it is a nest of thin deep-fried noodles that go soft where the sauce lands and stay crunchy elsewhere. Eat fast.

items.ja: 炸醤麺（ジャージャーメン）
items.en: Noodles topped with a salty minced-pork miso
items.note: Zha jiang mian — boiled noodles under a dark, intensely savoury meat-and-bean-paste sauce. Stir it all through before eating.
Add ¥200 for 大盛り (oomori, large) on any noodle dish here.
Plain unseasoned rice — genuinely gluten-free and vegan. Ask for it not fried and with no sauce and it is the one safe order in the building.
Soy-seasoned, with egg and pork through it.

items.en: House rice bowl — pork, vegetables and egg stir-fried over rice
items.note: The dish the shop is known for and the reason locals come. Pork, cabbage, carrot, onion, wood-ear and egg in a soy-and-oyster-sauce glaze, poured over a very large amount of rice. Portions here are famously enormous.

items.en: Mixed stir-fry in thick gravy over rice
items.note: 八宝菜 = 'eight treasures': pork, squid, prawn, cabbage, carrot, quail egg and so on in a starch-thickened sauce, ladled over rice.

items.en: Crab omelette over rice with sweet-sour gravy
items.note: A Japan-invented Chinese dish, and a comfort-food benchmark — a soft egg blanket over rice with a glossy, slightly sweet vinegared sauce.
Numbing-spicy tofu and pork mince on rice.

items.ja: 天津焼めし（塩あんかけ）
items.en: Crab omelette over fried rice with a salt-based gravy
items.note: The house mash-up: tenshin on top of fried rice instead of plain rice, with the clear salty gravy rather than the sweet one. Rice bowls are +¥200 for 大盛り (large).

items.en: Chinese set meal — crab omelette, mixed stir-fry and fried chicken with rice
items.note: Three mains on one plate plus a mountain of rice, for under ¥1,000. A blogger described needing a serious appetite to finish it.

items.en: 'Student set part 1' — crab omelette and Genghis-Khan mutton
items.note: The menu really does run 学生定食 parts I, II and III, all ¥950 — a relic of feeding hungry students. Part II is fish fry with pork-egg-vegetable stir-fry; part III is crab omelette with pork-and-cabbage miso stir-fry.

items.en: House set meal — sweet-sour pork, crab omelette and fried chicken
items.note: The greatest-hits plate. Three of the kitchen's best dishes side by side with rice.

items.en: Chinese bento A — sweet-sour fried chicken, crab omelette, shumai
items.note: 弁当 here is a compartmented lacquer tray, not a takeaway box. B (¥1,400) swaps in grilled pork loin; C (¥1,500) has tonkatsu and beef-and-aubergine.
Startlingly cheap. Wheat skins, soy in the filling, soy-vinegar dip — the classic celiac trap dish.
Thin wheat wrapper gathered around a pork-and-onion filling, steamed rather than fried.
骨なし = boneless; the menu also lists 骨付き (bone-in) at the same price. Choose by how much work you want to do.
The menu glosses it itself: 鶏素揚げ甘酢がけ — chicken deep-fried undredged, then drenched in sweet vinegar sauce.

kyr_ramen_henteko.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Read from a photograph of the touchscreen ticket machine whose own clock reads 2025/07/17.

items.en: HOW TO ORDER: buy a ticket from the machine just inside the door, then hand it over at the counter
items.section: はじめに / Before you order
items.note: It is a touchscreen machine with photographs, a Language button in the top right, and an eat-in / takeaway toggle. Pick your bowl, press 発券 (hassuken) to print the ticket, take your change. Extra toppings added later at your seat are paid in CASH at the counter, not on the machine.

items.en: House soy-sauce ramen on a rich chicken-paitan broth
items.note: The shop's flagship and the one to order first. Chicken feet plus small bones and aromatics simmered about six hours into a thick, creamy 鶏白湯 (tori-paitan), finished with a soy tare. The owner trained at Meimon, ancestor of Kyoto's famously heavy kotteri style.

items.en: Salt version of the house chicken-paitan ramen
items.note: Same six-hour chicken broth, salt tare instead of soy — sweeter and more directly chicken-flavoured.

items.en: Chicken-paitan ramen boosted with fish powder and bonito oil
items.note: The shop's own best-seller. An in-house blend of dried-fish powder and katsuo (bonito) oil stirred into the soy bowl — creamy and oceanic at once, with a deliberately retro set of toppings.

items.en: Chicken-paitan ramen with roasted dried-sardine paste
items.note: Niboshi roasted then ground into a house paste — bitter, dark and concentrated, cut by the creamy chicken base. Served with flat noodles rather than the usual round ones.

The opposite of the paitan bowls: several kinds of chicken bone, several dried fish and dried shiitake drawn out slowly at low temperature into a clear 清湯 (chintan) soup, with a slightly sweet house soy kaeshi and thin springy noodles. Topped with chashu, menma, negi and — rare in Kansai — なると (naruto, the pink-swirled fish cake).

items.ja: のすたるじっく冷やし中華
items.note: Summer only. Chilled noodles with cucumber, egg and pork in a tart dressing — the flavour Japanese adults associate with childhood summers.

items.en: Limited special A — the rotating experimental bowl
items.note: 限定 (gentei) = limited. The owner is a restless experimenter, so there is nearly always a 限定A and 限定B on the machine and no way to know in advance what they are — look at the posters on the wall by the door. Past ones: chilled mapo ramen, sake-lees ramen, a Jiro-style prawn-miso bowl, a carbonara bowl. Sells out.

items.en: Limited special B — second rotating bowl
items.note: Usually the pricier of the two limiteds. A red SOLD OUT overlay appears on the machine when it is gone — often by early afternoon.

items.en: Chilled mapo ramen — an example of a recent 限定A
items.note: House chilli oil and mapo mince over a cold soy-milk base with medium-thick curly noodles — ¥1,200 for 150g of noodles. Shown here as an example of what the 限定 slot looks like; it will not always be on.

items.ja: 墨染テコ系らーめん（泡）
items.en: House take on iekei ramen, foamed version — a recent limited
items.note: ¥1,200 for 150g of noodles, ¥1,300 for 220g. Thick chicken-paitan soy with spinach, wood-ear, naruto and the house chashu, whipped to a foam. Another example of the rotating limiteds.
+¥100 for the large. On the 魚介, 煮干し and 限定 bowls the surcharge is paid in cash directly at the counter, not on the ticket machine.
増 (mashi) = 'more of'. The cheapest way to change a bowl.
メンマ is bamboo shoot lacto-fermented then simmered — crunchy and sour-savoury. The simmering liquid is soy-based.
Braised pork, sliced. Soy-braised, so out on both counts.
Jammy yolk, steeped in soy tare. The universal ramen add-on — you will see 味玉 or 煮玉子 on almost every ramen menu in Japan.
Japanese kimchi often contains fish sauce or salted shrimp.

items.ja: 替え玉（定番しょうゆ・塩）
items.en: Refill of noodles, for the standard soy or salt bowls
items.note: 替え玉 (kaedama) means a second nest of noodles dropped into your remaining broth — the Kyushu habit, adopted widely. Leave enough soup. Order it at your seat and pay cash. For any bowl other than the standard soy or salt it is ¥150.

items.en: Lunch set: 2 pieces of fried chicken plus a medium rice
items.section: ランチタイムセット / Lunch sets (11:00-14:30)
items.note: Choose トリ唐 (tori-kara, plain fried chicken) or ヒリ唐 (hiri-kara, the spicy one), or a half-and-half. Upgrading the rice from 中 (medium) to 大 (large) is +¥50. Available 11:00-14:30 only.

items.en: Lunch set: a small rice bowl alongside your ramen
items.section: ランチタイムセット / Lunch sets (11:00-14:30)
items.note: Pick one of three: 炙りチャーシュー丼 (blowtorched pork over rice — wasabi on the side, ask them to leave it off if you would rather), ネギ塩レモンチャーシュー丼 (with salted spring onion and lemon), or カルボTKG (a carbonara-ish raw-egg rice).

items.ja: 卓上調味料（おろしにんにく・一味・コショウ・唐揚げの塩・七味）
items.en: On-table seasonings: grated garlic, chilli powder, pepper, seasoned salt for the fried chicken, seven-spice
items.note: Free to use. The garlic paste is what regulars stir into the paitan bowls. 一味 (ichimi) is pure chilli; 七味 (shichimi) is the seven-spice blend with citrus peel and sesame.

kyr_ramen_viska.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Taken from the shop's own blog and its newest wall boards, August 2026. A 2024 board circulating online prices the kotteri ¥100 lower and still shows the old Jiro call system — it is obsolete.

items.en: WHICH BOWLS ARE ON TODAY: check before you go
items.section: はじめに / Before you order
items.note: This is a one-man counter of 7 seats in a converted snack bar. The kotteri-based bowls (こってり, ビス郎, 汁無) are made on an irregular schedule because of prep constraints, while あっさり and クリアビス郎 run every open day. The owner posts the exact list for each stretch of days on his own note blog and on X/Instagram — worth a look the morning of. Sells out early on some days.

items.ja: こってり（超超濃厚豚骨）
items.note: ¥1,050 for 並 (nami, regular, 150g of noodles), ¥1,150 for 大 (dai, large, 225g). The shop's headline bowl and genuinely one of the thickest tonkotsu broths in a city that specialises in thick broths — closer to gravy than soup, clinging to medium-thick straight noodles. こってり literally means rich or heavy; あっさり is its opposite.

items.ja: あっさり（透き通る豚骨）
items.note: ¥1,100 regular (150g), ¥1,200 large (225g). Two aged raw soy sauces from long-established Kyoto makers blended into the tare, plus kombu and bonito dashi and Okayama chicken. Comes with chashu, house-made wontons and spring onion. There is yuzu in it — say so when ordering if you dislike citrus.

¥1,200 regular (150g), ¥1,300 large (225g). The signature of the owner's previous shop, brought back — runner-up in the chicken-paitan category of the 2018 Kansai Ultimate Ramen Award. The price includes an ajitama; ¥100 off if you do not want it. Contains yuzu.

items.ja: 極濃煮干し中華そば（限定）
items.note: ¥1,150 regular (150g), ¥1,250 large (225g), ¥1,050 mini (75g) — the mini is a rare and useful option if you want to try two things. Toppings for this bowl: 2 extra wontons ¥100, extra pork ¥300, extra onion ¥50. The shop recommends its 和え玉 (ae-dama) — a pre-seasoned second nest of noodles you eat separately rather than dropping into the soup.

items.en: House Jiro-style ramen — a mountain of beansprouts, cabbage, back-fat and pork over very fat noodles
items.section: マシマシ系（二郎系）/ Jiro-style
items.note: ¥1,200 for 並 = 300g of noodles. IMPORTANT and unusual: this shop is コール不要 — you do NOT have to shout the Jiro call. At a standard Jiro-style shop staff ask ニンニク入れますか (garlic in?) and you answer with some combination of ニンニク (garlic) / ヤサイ (extra veg) / アブラ (extra back-fat) / カラメ (stronger seasoning), plus 少なめ (less), マシ (more), マシマシ (loads). Here garlic, veg and fat are all self-service at the counter — take what you like. Noodle weight can be tuned in 10g steps at ±¥10 per 10g, with no upper limit.

items.en: Brothless Jiro-style — the same pile with no soup
items.section: マシマシ系（二郎系）/ Jiro-style
items.note: 汁無し = no soup. Sauce and oil sit at the bottom; mix hard from underneath before eating.
